name: GHRP-6

lead: GHRP-6 is a synthetic hexapeptide from the first generation of growth hormone releasing peptides. It was a research tool in the 1980s and 1990s and is now sold as a research chemical.
It is known for raising growth hormone and also for a strong hunger effect. Human evidence of improved muscle or appearance has not been published.

paras: GHRP-6 activates the ghrelin receptor, causing growth hormone release and appetite stimulation, and also raises cortisol and prolactin somewhat.
It is not approved for human use and is banned in sport. Reported effects include intense hunger, water retention and flushing. Long-term safety is unknown and quality is unregulated.

lead: GHRP-6 (growth hormone-releasing peptide 6, developmental code SKF-110679) is a synthetic hexapeptide with the sequence His-D-Trp-Ala-Trp-D-Phe-Lys-NH2. It belongs to a family of met-enkephalin analogues containing unnatural D-amino acids that lack opioid activity but strongly stimulate growth hormone (GH) release, and it was the first hexapeptide extensively studied in humans.[1][2][3]

GHRP-6 acts through a receptor distinct from the one used by growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). That receptor, originally named the growth hormone secretagogue receptor, is now recognised as the ghrelin receptor, which is why GHRP-6 is described as a synthetic ghrelin mimetic.[1][4] In addition to releasing GH, it stimulates appetite and raises cortisol, ACTH and prolactin to some degree.[5][6]

GHRP-6 has been used mainly as a research and diagnostic tool, including in provocative tests for adult GH deficiency, and it is sold as a research chemical to bodybuilders and others. It is not approved as a treatment, is prohibited in sport, and no published trial has shown improved muscle or appearance in healthy people.[7][8]

paras: GHRP-6 binds the ghrelin receptor in the pituitary and hypothalamus, stimulating pulsatile GH release independent of the GHRH pathway, with secondary appetite stimulation attributed to central ghrelin-like action and signalling through phospholipase C and calcium.[1][2] Reviews from the 1990s state that GHRPs have no sequence similarity to GHRH, act via specific pituitary and hypothalamic receptors, and may oppose somatostatin and work in part through GHRH release, though the exact mechanism was then unsettled.[3][9][10] Signal transduction by secretagogues raises intracellular calcium in somatotrophs whereas GHRH acts through cAMP.[4] Early cell studies reported that a related hexapeptide acted synergistically with GHRH on GH release from rat pituitary cells.[11]
Wikipedia states that giving GHRP-6 with insulin enhances the GH response, while eating carbohydrates or fats around the time of administration blunts GH release.[1]

Studies in rats show that GHRP-6 and ghrelin activate hypothalamic appetite-regulating neurons and induce feeding after central administration, and systemic GHRP-6 induces Fos and related proteins in the arcuate nucleus.[6][12] In people, a review notes GHRPs have significant prolactin and ACTH/cortisol-releasing effects and affect food intake and sleep.[5] A study in hyperthyroid patients compared ghrelin- and GHRP-6-induced ACTH and cortisol release to controls.[13]
GHRP-6 has been studied in human volunteers and patient groups mainly as a physiological probe of the GH axis rather than as a treatment.

Diagnosis of GH deficiency: Consensus reviews describe combined GHRH plus GH secretagogue tests, including GHRP-6, as maximal provocative tests for adult GH deficiency with defined, reproducible cut-offs able to distinguish normal from deficient subjects.[7]

Obesity and diabetes: GH secretion is markedly blunted in obesity. In obese patients GHRP-6 and hexarelin elicit greater GH responses than GHRH, though lower than in lean subjects, and the combination of GHRH and GHRP-6 is described as the most powerful GH-releasing stimulus known in obesity, though still less effective than in lean subjects.[14] Further studies examined GH response to GHRH plus GHRP-6 in type 2 diabetes under glucose clamps and the effect of lowering free fatty acids on blunted GH secretion in obesity.[15][16]
Pharmacokinetics: A pharmacokinetic study of GHRP-6 has been published.[17]

Cardiovascular: Receptor binding studies found GHRP binding sites in human heart and vascular tissue, with GHRP-6 able to inhibit radioligand binding, and reviewers have discussed possible cardiovascular effects of GHRPs.[5]

Wikipedia notes that a study in normal mice found differences in body composition, muscle growth, glucose metabolism, memory and cardiac function with GHRP-6 administration, and states many questions remain about the compound.[1]
No published human trial has tested GHRP-6 for muscle gain, fat loss or cosmetic outcomes in healthy people.

Documented effects of GHRP-6 include strong appetite stimulation and elevations of cortisol, ACTH and prolactin, which distinguish it from newer, more selective secretagogues.[5][2] Long-term safety in humans is not established; most published work involves single doses or short experiments in a research setting. Products sold as research chemicals are unregulated, and a 2023 analytical paper treats GHRP and GHRH peptides as doping substances requiring analytical standards for detection.[8]

GHRP-6 emerged from Cyril Bowers' work on synthetic peptides that release GH, which led to the search for the receptor distinct from the GHRH receptor and eventually to the identification of ghrelin as its natural ligand.[4][3] Non-peptide mimetics such as L-692,429 and MK-0677 were later discovered using GHRP-6 as a template, with the design of MK-0677 reported in 1995, and subsequent peptide analogues include GHRP-1, GHRP-2 and hexarelin.[9][3][18]

GHRP-6 is classified among the growth hormone-releasing peptides that anti-doping laboratories test for, and analytical methods exist to detect GHRPs and their metabolites.[8] Its appetite-stimulating effect, documented in animal and human work, is the property most often associated with it.[6][5]

timeline.event: Early rat pituitary cell work reports synergy between a GHRP hexapeptide and GHRH.[11]
Design and activity of the orally active non-peptide secretagogue MK-0677 reported.[18]
